ART ROOM LESSON · ART ROOM · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Glue — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson introduces glue through its card activity — making a paper collage — and installs the two rules that keep every future craft day sane: dots not rivers, press and wait.

What is this?

White glue is a liquid that grips by drying: its water evaporates, the rest hardens, and two things stay joined. It is the connective tissue of the whole art shelf.

What does it mean?

A collage teaches arrangement — which piece goes where, what touches what — and glue adds the discipline of waiting: the pieces only stay if the hands give them time.

What does the child need to know?

White glue, paper pieces (torn magazine pages work beautifully), and a base sheet. Glue sticks are tidier for tiny hands; the bottle is better for teaching the dot.

Why this matters

Collage is composition without drawing skills — anyone can arrange — so it gives every child a full art win. And learning that wet glue needs time is the child’s first material science: change takes a while.

What it teaches

Arrangement and composition, glue-quantity judgment, patience for drying, tearing strength, and the two-hand coordination of hold-press-count.

Words to learn

gluedotcollagetearpresswaitdrystick

Say this to your child

“"Here is our glue — it is the helping liquid! A little dot... another dot... NO rivers today! Press the paper down — one, two, three... ten! Stuck! Now it needs time to dry. What goes on next?"”

Step by step

  1. Tear or cut the paper pieces first — a little pile of color.
  2. Say the rule together: dots, not rivers.
  3. Place one dot, press one piece, count to ten.
  4. Build the collage outward — big pieces first, small pieces in the gaps.
  5. Leave it flat to dry and guess how long — then check the guess later.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a purple glue bottle stands ready with one drop at the tip — one drop is the whole message: glue is powerful, so it travels in small amounts.

Ask your child

"How much glue — a dot or a river?" (a dot) "What does glue do when it dries?" (hardens, grips) "What happens if we use too much?" (wrinkles, sliding pieces) "How long should we wait?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may squeeze the entire bottle given one unsupervised second, learn the dot rule in a single session, or press each piece down for a full solemn ten-count — the counting is optional but the pride is not.

Out in the real world

Bookbinders, carpenters, shoe makers and envelope factories all glue for a living — glued things hold the world together, from book spines to the envelope on the mail.

Try it together

Glue-dot dodge: the grown-up makes a "river" of glue on scrap paper and the child fixes it — "too much! dots!" — with their own correct version. Teaching the rule back proves it stuck.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me a glue dot." "What do we do after pressing the paper down?" (wait) "Why did our pieces slide?" (too much glue)

This lesson pairs with the Glue flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Art Room.
